name: Burdock root hair oil

lead: Burdock root hair oil, sometimes called bur oil, is an oil in which burdock root (Arctium) is infused, used as a scalp and hair treatment in European herbal tradition. Users apply it for scalp condition, shine and softness, and some hope for thicker-looking hair.

The appearance payoff users describe is a conditioned scalp and glossier strands. Reference works note its use as a scalp treatment in Europe, while no human trials of burdock oil for hair growth were identified.

paras: It is typically massaged into the scalp and lengths as a pre-wash treatment or leave-in conditioner, often alone or blended into other herbal hair oils such as castor or rosemary. Users commonly apply it for a few weeks or more before judging changes.

Burdock plants contain lactones that can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive people, and burdock is sometimes advised against during pregnancy. Patch-testing any new oil is common precaution on product labels.

chain: Conditioned scalp and shinier, softer hair
angle.text: Users rub burdock oil into the scalp and hair as a conditioning treatment. They are aiming at a healthier scalp environment and softer, glossier hair, with some hoping for a fuller look.

lead: Burdock root hair oil is an herbal oil made from the root of burdock plants (genus Arctium), used on the scalp and hair in European folk practice.[1]

People use it to condition the scalp and add softness and shine, and some hope it supports the look of thicker hair. Herbal reference works describe burdock root oil extract as a scalp treatment in Europe.[1]

paras: Burdock is a biennial plant whose root has been used as food and in herbal medicine. The seeds of Arctium lappa are used in traditional Chinese medicine as niubangzi, and the root is described as a traditional herb for many ailments.[1] Burdock root oil extract, called bur oil, is used in Europe as a scalp treatment.[1]
The root contains inulin, a prebiotic fiber, along with dietary fiber, minerals, amino acids and polyphenols.[1]

The above-ground green parts of burdock may cause contact dermatitis in allergic people, attributed to lactones.[1] Burdock is also sometimes advised against during pregnancy because animal studies showed uterine stimulation.[1]
